clue.text: Commander as sir ordering fellow-soldiers

indicators.note: to order things is to arrange them in a sequence, so the letters of the three words before it are put into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written: fourteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An officer, addressed as sir, barks commands at the troops who serve together under him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordering' looks like the commander issuing orders, but it is the anagram signal: the fourteen letters of COMMANDER AS SIR are put in a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: A set phrase for people who serve and fight side by side in the same army, so a straight synonym.

clue.text: Weight of dozen getiing bigger!

parts.note: the weight 'of dozen' is the two-letter abbreviation oz printed inside that word; getting bigger (misprinted 'getiing' here) means writing the abbreviation out in full

explanation.surface: Twelve of something are growing, and together they weigh more and more.
explanation.walkthrough: No twelve things are being weighed. Look inside the word dOZen for the abbreviation of a weight, then let it 'get bigger' by spelling it out in full.
explanation.definitionFit: An imperial unit of weight, one sixteenth of a pound, whose abbreviation oz is found inside the word dozen.

clue.text: Rodent on bark of oak, maybe, or palm

indicators.note: in a down clue a piece written on another sits above it, so the rodent comes first and the bark follows below

parts.note: a rat is a common rodent
tan is the crushed bark of oak or other trees used for tanning leather; maybe admits oak is just one source

explanation.surface: Some small gnawing animal is sitting on the bark of a tree, perhaps an oak, perhaps a palm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or palm' looks like a second tree for the rodent to sit on, but it is the definition. The bark is the kind tanners use, and 'on' means above in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A climbing palm of tropical Asia whose long stems are made into cane furniture, so the definition names its plant family.

clue.text: Scorn's curtailed when sweetheart's brought around tea

indicators.note: the sweetheart word is brought around the shortened scorn word, so it goes on the outside and encloses it

parts.note: darling is what you call a sweetheart

indicators.note: to curtail is to cut short, so the word for scorn loses its last letter

parts.note: to jeer is to scorn or mock openly, and a jeer is a scornful taunt

explanation.surface: A fit of sneering is cut short the moment a loved one comes round with a pot of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a sweetheart delivering tea, but 'brought around' makes the endearment enclose the scorn word, which 'curtailed' has cut down to JEE. The definition is the single last word.
explanation.definitionFit: A fine black tea grown in the Himalayan foothills of West Bengal, so the definition names the general drink.

clue.text: Storage unit contaminated with oils

indicators.note: something contaminated is spoiled and no longer in its pure state, so the letters of the word that follows are disturbed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A storage tank has been polluted by leaking oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contaminated' is the anagram signal working on OILS; 'with' merely joins the two.
explanation.definitionFit: A tower or pit on a farm for keeping grain or fodder, so an example of a place where things are stored.

clue.text: A very small thing — one won't be charged

definitions.text: A very small thing — one won't be charged

parts.words: A very small thing — one won't be charged
parts.note: charged is meant electrically, not as a bill to pay: this describes a subatomic particle that carries no electric charge

explanation.surface: Something so tiny that the shop will not bother asking you to pay for it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about a trifle you get for free. Read 'charged' as electric charge and the small thing becomes a particle that has none.
explanation.definitionFit: A subatomic particle found in the atomic nucleus, tiny and electrically neutral, so both halves describe it.

clue.text: Pursuit of Saracens leading to one country's downfall

indicators.note: the first piece leads to the others, so it is written first and they follow it

parts.note: Saracens are an English rugby union club, so their pursuit, meaning their game, is rugby union, abbreviated RU
the Roman numeral for one is I
a nation is a country

explanation.surface: Crusaders chasing a Saracen army end up bringing a whole kingdom to its knees.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Crusaders hunting medieval Muslim armies. Saracens is an English rugby union club, so their 'pursuit' is the sport, RU; 'leading to' puts it in front.
explanation.definitionFit: The act of wrecking something or the state of being wrecked, a synonym for a collapse from power or prosperity.

clue.text: Soppy person made one mad — it's ridiculous

parts.note: to send someone into a state is to make them that way, as in 'the noise sent him crazy'
the Roman numeral for one is I
mental is British slang for mad or crazy

indicators.note: something ridiculous makes no sense, so the letters of the word before it are jumbled out of order

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A mawkish individual drove somebody up the wall, and the speaker finds the whole business absurd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made one mad' is read word by word as SENT I MENTAL, since what sends you mental makes you mad. 'ridiculous' jumbles IT'S into IST.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone given to mawkish, excessive tender feeling; soppy is British slang for foolishly tender or tearful.

clue.text: Accepted as something worth discussing (minutes earlier?)

definitions.text: Accepted as something worth discussing (minutes earlier?)

parts.words: Accepted as something worth discussing (minutes earlier?)
parts.note: minutes here are the written record of the last meeting, which a committee takes first; an item accepted for discussion is listed after them in the order of business

explanation.surface: An idea was agreed to be worth talking about, perhaps only a few minutes before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minutes earlier' is not about time. At a formal meeting the minutes, the record of the previous meeting, come first, and topics accepted for discussion are listed after them.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic formally listed for a meeting has been accepted for debate, and the previous meeting's minutes normally come before it.

clue.text: A French sign in bar? Strange

parts.note: un is the French word for 'a'
in written music a natural is the sign placed before a note in a bar to cancel a sharp or flat; the question mark admits it is one sign of several

explanation.surface: A notice written in French hanging in a pub strikes someone as odd.
explanation.walkthrough: The bar is a bar of written music, not a pub: the sign is the one that cancels a sharp or flat.
explanation.definitionFit: Something contrary to the normal order of things is odd or abnormal, so the two adjectives are close synonyms.

clue.text: Group who may want better conditions in marriage

definitions.text: Group who may want better conditions
definitions.meaning: an organised body of workers that bargains with employers for better pay and working conditions
the joining of two people as spouses, which this word formally describes

explanation.surface: People who would like their married life to be happier than it is.
explanation.walkthrough: The conditions belong to a workplace, not a marriage: the first definition is a body of organised workers, and 'in' merely links it to the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Workers band together in one to bargain with employers, and a wedding joins two people in one: both are a coming together.

clue.text: Old woman having good energy? Too old!

indicators.note: the old woman has the next two pieces, so they are added after her name

parts.note: O is a standard abbreviation for old, as in OT for Old Testament
Vera is a woman's name; crosswords often clue a first name simply as woman or girl
G is the abbreviation for good, as in a grade or a coin's condition
E is the physicist's symbol for energy, as in E = mc squared

explanation.surface: An elderly lady is surprisingly sprightly, though someone still thinks she is past it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old woman' looks like one unit, but it splits into O and the name VERA; 'having' just attaches G and E. The word old appears twice: once as a letter, once in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective for someone beyond the permitted or suitable age limit, as an athlete barred from a junior event would be.

clue.text: A silly girl, a sheep

indicators.note: silly here means muddled or senseless, telling you the letters that follow it are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written and mixed in with the letters of girl

explanation.surface: A foolish girl is dismissed as a sheep, someone who just follows the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a sheep' wants to be the definition, but that leaves the anagram a letter short: the second 'a' is fodder too. 'silly' stirs it in with the word before the comma, making RGALI after the opening A.
explanation.definitionFit: The large wild sheep of the Central Asian mountains, with huge curling horns, so the definition names its kind.

clue.text: Eastern chap given call, the old man imprisoned being set free

indicators.note: the eastern chap is given the next part, which is added after him

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for east or eastern, as on a compass
chap is informal British for a man

indicators.note: the old man is imprisoned, that is shut up inside, the word for call

parts.note: to cite someone is to call or summon them, for instance to appear in court
the old man is slang for your father, and pa is a familiar word for father

explanation.surface: A man from the East gets a phone call saying his jailed father is being released.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface tells of a jailed father being released, so 'imprisoned' and 'set free' seem to go together. They do different jobs: 'imprisoned' is the container signal, 'given' simply adds the next piece, and 'set free' is a verb, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To release someone from slavery, bondage or legal restraint, a formal synonym of liberate.

clue.text: Understanding secured, we hear

indicators.note: we hear tells you the word for secured is listened to rather than read, and a word that sounds the same is written in

parts.note: tacked means fastened with tacks, which are small nails, or with loose temporary stitches

explanation.surface: Word reaches us that some agreement has been reached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' marks a soundalike: TACKED, fastened with small nails, is pronounced exactly like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A sensitive feel for what to say or do without giving offence, which is one kind of sympathetic awareness of others.

clue.text: Being modest about page — just a property of the author?

indicators.note: the modest word goes about, that is around, the abbreviation for page

parts.note: someone being modest or shy is coy
p is the standard abbreviation for page, as in p. 12
just means fair or morally right, as in a just decision

explanation.surface: A writer is bashful about one sheet of the book, which is simply how that writer is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'just a property' reads as 'merely a trait of the writer', but 'just' is a separate piece meaning fair, and the property is legal ownership. 'about' makes the modest word enclose the page.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclusive legal right to reproduce a work, which belongs to its writer as intellectual possession.

clue.text: Darling girl, a juicy type

definitions.meaning: the miner's daughter of the American folk ballad whose chorus begins 'Oh my darling, oh my darling'
a small, sweet, easily peeled citrus fruit, a cross between a mandarin and an orange

explanation.surface: A sweet young woman who is also rather a luscious sort.
explanation.walkthrough: Neither half is about a person's charms: the first points to the girl of the Gold Rush ballad 'Oh My Darling', the second to a fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The folk ballad addresses its drowned heroine as 'my darling', and her name is also that of a small sweet citrus fruit.

clue.text: Justifying the kicked-out lover? Unlovely at home, not much good!

parts.note: an ex is a former partner, here imagined as one who has been shown the door
plain is a polite word for not good-looking
in means at home, as in 'is anyone in?'

indicators.note: not much of the word that follows is wanted: only its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone defends throwing out a partner who was unattractive around the house and generally useless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not much good' is no verdict on the lover: 'not much' asks for only the first letter of GOOD. The definition is the single opening word.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving the reasons for your conduct is a way of accounting for or defending it, so a near synonym.

clue.text: Brings gas into set area with new development

indicators.note: the two words before it are given a new development, that is built afresh in a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gas main is being laid to a designated zone where new houses are going up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with new development' is the anagram signal: SET AREA is rebuilt. The definition is a verb in the third person, hence the final S.
explanation.definitionFit: To charge a liquid or soil with air or carbon dioxide is to introduce a gas to it; the verb is in the third person.

clue.text: Bird's speed

definitions.meaning: a small grey wading bird of the sandpiper family that winters on British estuaries
a ship's or aircraft's rate of travel of one nautical mile per hour

explanation.definitionFit: A small sandpiper that winters on estuaries and a rate of one nautical mile an hour share this name.

clue.text: A cross that's primarily a lucky charm

parts.note: a mule is a cross, the hybrid offspring of a male donkey and a female horse

indicators.note: primarily, meaning first of all, points to the opening letter of the word just before it

explanation.surface: A crucifix that someone wears mainly for good luck.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross is not a crucifix but a hybrid animal, MULE. 'primarily' takes the first letter of THAT'S.
explanation.definitionFit: A small object worn to ward off evil or bring good fortune, in other words a talisman.

clue.text: Man to draw back when her majesty enters

indicators.note: her majesty enters, that is goes inside, the turned-round word for draw
back tells you the word for draw is written from its last letter to its first

parts.note: to drag is to draw or pull something along
ER, for Elizabeth Regina, was the royal cipher of Queen Elizabeth II

explanation.surface: A gentleman is expected to step back respectfully when the Queen comes into the room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draw back' looks like one verb, to retreat, but the words work separately: 'back' turns the synonym for draw into GARD, and the royal cipher 'enters' that. The man is simply a first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A male first name, borne for instance by the poet Gerard Manley Hopkins, so the answer is one example of a man.

clue.text: One taking test collecting two marks? That's bad!

indicators.note: the pieces before it collect the marks, gathering them up inside themselves
one takes the test, so the word for test is attached straight after it

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
an oral is a spoken exam, such as a language test

indicators.note: two tells you the abbreviation for mark is written twice over

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for mark, the former German currency

explanation.surface: A candidate sits an exam and comes away with only two marks, a dreadful result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two' doubles M (mark, old German currency), 'collecting' puts that pair inside I plus ORAL, which 'taking' joins. 'bad' means wicked, not a poor score.
explanation.definitionFit: Conduct that goes against accepted standards of right and wrong is wicked, a synonym in the ethical sense.

clue.text: Member of group gets to call round

parts.note: to ring someone is British for to telephone or call them
the letter O is a round shape, so round can stand for it

explanation.surface: Someone in a club has the job of phoning round the others.
explanation.walkthrough: The group is the Beatles, whose drummer was Ringo Starr. 'to call round' looks like visiting, but splits into RING (telephone) and the round letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: The stage name of Richard Starkey, drummer of the Beatles, so he is one example of somebody belonging to a band.

clue.text: Aboard boat there's hard criminal

indicators.note: aboard means on or in a vessel, so the piece after the boat is put inside the boat word

parts.note: a tug is a small powerful boat that tows larger ships
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils graded H or HB

explanation.surface: A hardened crook is on board a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aboard' is the container signal: H goes inside TUG. 'hard' seems to describe the criminal but is the pencil grade.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent ruffian, typically one who robs or beats people for a gang, so a kind of lawbreaker.

clue.text: Near back of hut it's dark

parts.note: nigh is an old or poetic word for near, as in 'the end is nigh'

indicators.note: the back of a word is its rear end, so only the last letter of the next word is used

explanation.surface: Round behind the shed there is no light at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back of' takes the last letter of HUT. 'Near' is not a position but the old word NIGH, and 'it's' just links to the definition, 'dark' as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, dark means the hours after sunset when there is no daylight, as in 'home before dark'.

clue.text: Starts of newspaper articles responsible for furrows on brows?

definitions.meaning: the large-type titles printed above news stories, where each story begins
wrinkles across the forehead: a whimsical two-word description, the question mark admitting it is not a dictionary phrase

explanation.surface: The opening paragraphs of news stories are enough to make readers frown with worry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts of' looks like an instruction to take first letters, but it is a straight definition. 'responsible for' links it to a pun: split in two, the answer describes wrinkles on a forehead.
explanation.definitionFit: The titles that open news stories; split in two, the word whimsically describes wrinkles across the forehead.

clue.text: 'Why not buy a Ferrari?' — result of hypnotism?

definitions.meaning: a quoted example of advice about which car to get; a car is an automobile, so this is a recommendation about a motor
the planting of an idea in your own mind so that it shapes your behaviour, a process akin to self-hypnosis; the question mark covers the looseness

explanation.surface: Somebody floats the idea of buying a sports car and wonders whether hypnosis put it into their head.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer after its first four letters and the quoted question becomes an example: a piece of advice about a car. The second definition is the real word, loosely given.
explanation.definitionFit: The quoted question is a playful example of advice about a car, and the real word names self-induced persuasion akin to hypnosis.
